findings.description:
The new scrubber can discard executable content that is executed within the same Bash invocation. For example: `tee /tmp/payload <<'EOF'
if true; then rm -rf / --no-preserve-root; fi
EOF
bash /tmp/payloa?`. Assuming the glob resolves to the newly written file, `_bdb_hd_same_line_exec` misses the execution because it searches for the literal basename `payload`. `_bdb_hd_scan_body` then discards all three segments beginning with `if`, `then`, and `fi`, removing the destructive command from the scan.
findings.failure_mode: A destructive command previously visible to the fence disappears from `_cmd_match`, while Bash subsequently executes it. This bypass occurs within one invocation, outside the documented limitation concerning execution by a later command.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the full heredoc body whenever another command in the invocation can execute a file and its target cannot be resolved conclusively. Also treat shell compound-command keywords in heredoc bodies as requiring the full scan. Add a regression case covering execution through a glob.

findings.description: The per-segment body scan (_bdb_hd_scan_body -> _bdb_hd_segword) only strips `( { ! \ " '`, assignments, and the sudo/env-style wrapper list before reading the command word. Shell keywords that routinely precede a command on the same segment are NOT stripped: `then`, `do`, `else`, `elif`, `if`, `while`, `until`, and case arms like `*)`. A body line `if true; then rm -rf /; fi` splits into segments `if true` / `then rm -rf /` / `fi`; the command word of the second is `then`, which is neither a fence verb nor an interpreter, so the segment is dropped. The same happens for `for f in *; do rm -rf "$f"; done`, `while :; do git push --force; done`, and `*) kubectl delete ns prod;;`. The header comment promises that "a segment whose command word is a fence verb ... is kept on its own line for the normal rules"; for the most common script shapes (if/for/while bodies) that promise is not met, and the fence rules never see the destructive command. Because the classifier is the default (knob on), this is a regression against the pre-cycle full scan for every heredoc that is classified nonexec but whose body is later executed within the same command through a path _bdb_hd_same_line_exec does not recognise (see DISS-002), e.g. `cat <<'EOF' > x` ... `eval "$(cat x)"`.
findings.failure_mode: A heredoc written with cat/tee to a non-executable-looking path and holding `if ...; then rm -rf ...; fi` (or any keyword-prefixed destructive segment) is scrubbed to nothing; the body is then executed in the same command via `eval "$(cat x)"`, `bash -c "$(<x)"` or `bash ./*`, and the destructive-command fence that previously matched `rm -rf` anywhere in the command text no longer fires.
findings.suggested_fix: In _bdb_hd_segword, add the shell keywords to the prefix-stripping set (`if|then|else|elif|fi|while|until|do|done|case|esac|select|in|time|coproc|function`) and strip a leading case-arm pattern (`*)`, `pattern)`). Alternatively, in _bdb_hd_scan_body set `_hd_full=1` whenever a segment's command word is a shell keyword, so the body falls back to the full scan. Add corpus cases for if/then, for/do and case-arm bodies under cat/tee heredocs.

findings.description: _bdb_hd_same_line_exec decides whether a heredoc's write target is executed elsewhere in the command by comparing token basenames to the target. Two blind spots let an executing reference through: (1) a target named inside a quoted substitution is one token, e.g. `eval "$(cat x)"` or `bash -c "$(<x)"`, whose stripped basename is `$(cat x)` and never equals `x`; _bdb_hd_ctx_bad treats `$(`/backtick/`<(` as unreadable, but this function does not. (2) `git` and `gh` are on the safe-reader list, yet `git -c core.sshCommand=./x fetch`, `git -c alias.r='!./x' r`, and `gh extension install ./x` run the named file. On their own these only matter when the body carries destructive text the per-segment scan drops (DISS-001), but they are the half of that bypass that makes the heredoc look nonexec.
findings.failure_mode: A cat/tee heredoc whose target is executed on the same command line via a quoted command substitution or a git -c/alias invocation is classified nonexec and its body is reduced to fence-verb segments instead of being scanned in full.
findings.suggested_fix: At the top of the per-line loop, return 0 (treat as executing) when a non-body line contains `$(`, a backtick, `<(` or `>(`, mirroring _bdb_hd_ctx_bad. Remove `git` and `gh` from _bdb_hd_is_safe_reader or restrict them to read-only subcommands (e.g. git add/diff/status/log, gh pr/issue view).

findings.description: Every allowlisted consumer is bumped to `interpreter` when any argument matches `_bdb_hd_re_exflag='^-[A-Za-z]*[cex][A-Za-z]*$'`. That regex also matches `jq -c`, `jq -e`, `jq -rc`, `yq -e`, `grep -c`, `grep -x`, `sed -n -e '1p'`, `cat -e` and `echo -e`. `jq -c '...' <<EOF` and `jq -e` are among the most common heredoc consumers in this codebase, so the FP-reduction the classifier exists for (#1245 class) is lost for them and the body is full-scanned exactly as before. It is safe, but it defeats the stated purpose for a large share of legitimate heredocs and will keep producing the same false positives the cycle set out to remove.
findings.failure_mode: Legitimate `jq -c`/`jq -e`/`grep -c` heredocs whose body mentions rm/git/kubectl text are still flagged by the fence; the classifier reports interpreter for them.
findings.suggested_fix: Apply the generic exec-flag check only to consumers without a dedicated argv grammar, or whitelist the known-harmless short flags per command (jq/yq: -c -e -r -S -s; grep: -c -x -E; sed: -e when the script still matches the print-only grammar) before falling through to the generic `[cex]` test.

findings.description: check_implement_marker is invoked as a bare statement followed by `marker_rc=$?`. Every other predicate in this hook is called inside `if`/`&&` and every assignment is guarded with `|| default`, which is the idiom used under `set -e`/`set -euo pipefail`. If the script (or a future edit) enables errexit, the common case (no marker file, return 1) aborts the hook with exit 1 and no stdout before any ask/deny/row is emitted, which Claude Code treats as a non-blocking error, i.e. the write is allowed. I could not see the shebang/set lines in the diff, so this is conditional on the script's option state.
findings.failure_mode: Under errexit the gate exits 1 on every unsanctioned write with no marker, producing neither an ask nor a deny nor an audit row; the write proceeds.
findings.suggested_fix: Call it as `if check_implement_marker; then marker_rc=0; else marker_rc=$?; fi` or `check_implement_marker && marker_rc=0 || marker_rc=$?`, matching the rest of the file.

findings.description: The new `sanctioned_marker` path allows every App Zone write for two hours in every mode, including `deny`, when `.run/implement-active.json` carries `{skill: implement|bug, sprint, started_at}`. The marker is added to the trust-input list, but that list only governs the Write/Edit hook. Nothing in this diff stops the model from producing the marker through Bash, either by running `run-checkpoint.sh mark implement <sprint>` outside any run or by `printf '{...}' > .run/implement-active.json`. The header describes deny mode as the one configuration where the gate "is a fence"; with a self-issuable sanction it is a fence against Write/Edit only. The same is true of the derived cache, but the marker is new, cheaper to forge (no derive step, no RUNNING state), and sanctions regardless of position.
findings.failure_mode: In deny mode a single Bash command creates a fresh marker, after which all App Zone writes are allowed with decision `sanctioned_marker` for two hours; the deny decision never fires.
findings.suggested_fix: Have `run-checkpoint.sh mark` refuse (or the gate ignore the marker) unless the derived cache is RUNNING and fresh, so the marker can only extend an existing run; and/or add `.run/implement-active.json` and `.run/sprint-plan-state.json` as write targets the Bash fence asks on, so Bash and Write/Edit are treated alike.

findings.description: Both skill includes now gate on a shell-out: `.claude/scripts/lib/profile-lib.sh knob <key> [fallback]` must print `true`. The retrospective postlude omits the fallback argument that input_guardrails.md passes, and both depend on profile-lib.sh being executable and supporting a `knob` CLI entry point alongside being sourceable (the hooks `source` it). profile-lib.sh is new and was not shown. Any mismatch (missing exec bit, `knob` requiring two args, a sourced-only lib) makes the command print nothing, and both includes fall open: guardrails are skipped and the retrospective never runs, silently, for every skill that embeds them.
findings.failure_mode: If the CLI contract differs from the include text, the invisible retrospective (standard profile: true) is never executed and input guardrails are never run, with no error surfaced.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass the fallback in the postlude too (`knob invisible_retrospective.enabled false`), confirm profile-lib.sh has the exec bit and a `[[ ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} == $0 ]]` CLI dispatcher accepting one or two args, and add a bats case that invokes the exact command string from each include.
